description: List recent Outlook inbox mail from MAIIC or Dr Thom with attachment counts
--- command ---
try { $ol = New-Object -ComObject Outlook.Application; $ns = $ol.GetNamespace("MAPI"); $inbox = $ns.GetDefaultFolder(6); $items = $inbox.Items; $items.Sort("[ReceivedTime]", $true); $n = 0; foreach ($m in $items) { if ($m.SenderEmailAddress -match "maiic|kumwenda" -or $m.SenderName -match "Kumwenda|Thom") { "{0} | {1} | {2} | att={3}" -f $m.ReceivedTime, $m.SenderName, $m.Subject, $m.Attachments.Count; $n++; if ($n -ge 25) { break } } } ; if ($n -eq 0) { "no MAIIC mail found in Outlook inbox" } } catch { "Outlook COM not available: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
{
 "timeout": 120000
}
````

<?php
namespace App\Services\Macro;
/**
 * Parses the IMF World Economic Outlook (WEO) dataset for a given macro
 * variable's indicator code and returns a normalised preview.
 *
 * Quirks of the WEO file:
 *   - Despite the `.xls` extension, the IMF publishes WEO as a tab-delimited
 *     UTF-16 LE text file (not real Excel). This parser handles that natively
 *     without needing PhpSpreadsheet.
 *   - "Estimates Start After" column (sometimes blank, often "n.a.") tells you
 *     which year is the first FORECAST year. Years <= that value are 'actual'
 *     (historical/observed), years > are 'forecast' (IMF projection).
 *   - The file covers every country × every indicator (~200k rows). We filter
 *     to ZMB + the chosen indicator before doing anything else.
 *
 * Source URL (no API key, download by hand and upload to the system):
 *   https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WEO/weo-database/
 */
````

    public function run(): void
    {
        foreach (self::WORLD_BANK as $code => $wbCode) {
            $variable = MacroVariable::where('code', $code)->first();
            if (! $variable) {
                continue;
            }
            $external = is_array($variable->external_codes) ? $variable->external_codes : [];
            $external['world_bank'] = $wbCode;
            $variable->update([
                'external_codes' => $external,
                'source' => $variable->source ?: 'World Bank Open Data',
            ]);
        }
    }
}

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 18:58:14 UTC)

Here is what ZNBS does and how MAIIC can adopt it. The fit is good: MAIIC already has the tables and the Forward-Looking screens; what it lacks is the ingestion and the preview-then-commit discipline.

## What the ZNBS macro ingestion is

- **Two external sources, no API keys.** `WorldBankFetcherService` pulls annual series from `api.worldbank.org/v2/country/{ISO3}/indicator/{CODE}` (60 s timeout, two retries, country from config with a UI override, year range optional). `ImfWeoParserService` reads the IMF World Economic Outlook file (which is tab-delimited UTF-16, not real Excel) and splits each year into *actual* or *forecast* using the "Estimates Start After" column — that is where the forecast periods come from.
- **Indicator codes live on the variable**, not in code: `macro_variables.external_codes = {"world_bank": "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"}`, seeded by `MacroExternalCodesSeeder` for nine indicators (GDP growth, CPI, exchange rate, unemployment, GNI per capita, reserves, debt/GDP, fiscal balance, private credit). A variable with no code shows "no indicator configured", not an error.
- **Preview, then commit.** The screen fetches a preview (`variables/{id}/preview-worldbank`), shows the rows, and only on "Import" writes to `macro_observations` (`import-worldbank`), under the `manage macro` permission; `view macro` can preview. Every import is a `SourceImportBatch` (source, URL, fetched-at, who, rows) — provenance for each observation.
- **Observations are keyed** on (variable, period_date, period_type) with `value`, mild and severe overrides, `source`, notes — so an API refresh upserts rather than duplicates.
- **A command for the bootstrap and the scheduler**: `macro:import-worldbank {--code=}` imports every variable that has a code, non-fatal per indicator, and `icaap:bootstrap` runs it.
- **The screen** (Data Foundation › Macro Statistics Manager) has five tabs: Dashboard, Variables, Data Entry, Table 9 · Assumptions (the governed base/mild/severe paths with approval lineage), Import / Export (World Bank with country + year range, IMF WEO upload, CSV template).

## What MAIIC has today

`macro_statistics` (code, name, unit, frequency, history/forecast period counts, source, website link) and `macro_statistics_data` (definition, scenario, period, value, `is_forecast`, `is_fli`, confidence bounds, assumptions, source), unique on (definition, period, scenario) — a close cousin of the ZNBS pair, and in one respect ahead of it (scenario on the row). Screens: Macro Elements (manual CRUD), Scenario Profiles, Weighted Forecast, Credit Loss Data, Adjusted Forecast, Regression. No external source, no preview, no provenance, no command.

## Suggested adoption

| # | Adopt | How, in MAIIC's terms |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Indicator codes on the variable** | Add `external_codes` (JSON) and `country` (default `MWI`) to `macro_statistics`; seed Malawi codes — GDP growth `NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG`, CPI `FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG`, MWK/USD `PA.NUS.FCRF`, lending rate `FR.INR.LEND`, real interest rate `FR.INR.RINR`, private credit `FS.AST.PRVT.GD.ZS`, **agriculture value-added growth `NV.AGR.TOTL.KD.ZG`** (MAIIC's book is agricultural and industrial), broad money growth `FM.LBL.BMNY.ZG`, reserves `FI.RES.TOTL.MO`, debt/GDP `GC.DOD.TOTL.GD.ZS`, current account `BN.CAB.XOKA.GD.ZS` |
| 2 | **The two fetchers and the batch table**, ported as they are | `WorldBankFetcherService`, `ImfWeoParserService`, `SourceImportBatch` into `app/Services/Macro`; `config/services.worldbank.country = MWI`; observations land in `macro_statistics_data` with `is_forecast` set from WEO's estimates-start year and `source_import_batch_id` on every row |
| 3 | **Preview, then commit, under permissions** | `macro.view` / `macro.manage` added to the role set; the same two endpoints per source |
| 4 | **The command and the schedule** | `macro:import-worldbank` run by `eir:bootstrap` and monthly by the scheduler; a committed JSON snapshot under `docs/bootstrap/macro/` as the offline fallback so a server with no internet still bootstraps |
| 5 | **Reserve Bank of Malawi series by file** | Policy rate and PLR are not on the World Bank; the PLR is already in the landing zone (`P2_06`), and the RBM policy rate comes by a small CSV through the same preview-commit screen — one more source tab, not a special case |
| 6 | **One governed rule for a disagreement** | A Governance Centre setting, `macro_source_precedence`: World Bank for actuals, IMF WEO for forecasts, RBM file for rates; a manual entry overrides either only with a reason |
| 7 | **The screen, in the suite layout** | Data Foundation › **Macro Statistics** with the five tabs; MAIIC's "Table 9" equivalent is **Scenario Assumptions** — the base/mild/severe paths that feed Scenario Profiles and the Weighted Forecast, with the same approval lineage. Regression, Weighted Forecast and Adjusted Forecast stay in Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking Model; the ingestion moves to Data Foundation, where the suite puts it |
| 8 | **Provenance to the audit workbook** | Every observation's batch (source, URL, fetched-at, who) is what the IFRS 9 impairment workbook cites for B5.5.49–54 (reasonable and supportable forward-looking information) |

Effort: about two days to port services, migration, seeder, command and tests; one day for the screen in the new layout; half a day for the snapshot and the audit rows. It sits naturally with UI-1/UI-2 since it is the first Data Foundation screen rebuilt in the suite shape.

## 13. Macro statistics: ingestion from the World Bank and the IMF

### 13.1 In plain language

The forward-looking part of IFRS 9 (B5.5.49 to B5.5.54) asks MAIIC to adjust its expected credit losses for what is reasonably expected to happen to the economy: growth, inflation, the exchange rate, interest rates, the harvest. Today those figures are typed into the system by hand from whatever source the analyst had open, with no record of where a number came from or when. The Dupleix suite does this differently: the system fetches the published series itself from the World Bank's open data service and the IMF's World Economic Outlook, shows the analyst what it found, and writes it only when the analyst says so, with the source, the address and the time kept against every figure. Decision D27 adopts that for MAIIC.

### 13.2 What MAIIC has today

The module exists and its tables are sound. `macro_statistics` holds the definition of each series (code, name, unit, frequency, how many historical and forecast periods, source, website link, active flag); `macro_statistics_data` holds one value per series, period and scenario, with an actual-or-forecast flag, an FLI flag, confidence bounds, assumptions and a free-text source, unique on series, period and scenario. Six screens use them under IFRS 9 Model Setup: Macro Elements (manual entry), Scenario Profiles, Weighted Forecast, Credit Loss Data, Adjusted Forecast and Regression Analysis, and the Management Overlays group holds the economic scenarios and external calculations.

What is missing is everything before the first screen: no external source, no preview before a write, no record of where a value came from, no command a bootstrap or a scheduler could run, and no rule for what happens when two sources disagree. The scenario-on-the-row design is in one respect ahead of the suite's and is kept.

### 13.3 What the suite does, and is adopted

| Element | What it does | MAIIC adoption |
|---|---|---|
| **Indicator codes on the series** | Each macro variable carries the external codes that identify it at each source (`external_codes`, for example `{"world_bank": "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"}`), seeded once. A series with no code says so on the screen; it is not an error | Two columns added to `macro_statistics`: `external_codes` (JSON) and `country` (ISO3, default `MWI`); a seeder with the Malawi codes of 13.4 |
| **World Bank fetcher** | Pulls an annual series for a country from `api.worldbank.org/v2/country/{ISO3}/indicator/{code}`: public, no key, 60-second timeout, two retries, year range optional, country from configuration with a screen override. Returns a normalised preview; writes nothing | `WorldBankFetcherService` ported as it is; `services.worldbank.country = MWI` |
| **IMF WEO parser** | Reads the World Economic Outlook download (a tab-delimited UTF-16 text file despite its `.xls` name), filters to the country and indicator, and marks each year actual or forecast from the "Estimates Start After" column. This is where the forecast periods come from | `ImfWeoParserService` ported; the file is uploaded by hand from the IMF site, which has no key-free API |
| **Preview, then commit** | Two endpoints per source: a preview the viewer may call, and a commit that writes, for the manager only. Nothing reaches the table until a person has seen the rows | Routes `macro-statistics.preview-worldbank`, `.import-worldbank`, `.preview-imf-weo`, `.import-imf-weo`; permissions `macro.view` and `macro.manage` added to the role set |
| **Provenance per import** | Every commit is a batch: source, address, fetched-at, who, how many rows, the file's hash where there is one; every observation points to its batch | `macro_source_import_batches`; `source_import_batch_id` on `macro_statistics_data`; the free-text `source` kept for manual entries |
| **Upsert, never duplicate** | Observations are keyed on series, period and period type, so a refresh updates the value and keeps the key | MAIIC's unique key on series, period and scenario already does this; an API import writes to the base scenario |
| **A command** | `macro:import-worldbank {--code=}` imports every series with a code, non-fatal per series, for the bootstrap and the scheduler | The same command; run by `eir:bootstrap` and monthly by the scheduler; a committed JSON snapshot under `docs/bootstrap/macro/` is the offline fallback so a server without internet still bootstraps |
| **The screen** | One page with five tabs: Dashboard, Variables, Data Entry, governed assumptions, Import / Export (World Bank with country and year range, IMF upload, CSV template and export) | Data Foundation, Macro Statistics (section 11.3), five tabs; the governed-assumptions tab is **Scenario Assumptions**, the base, mild and severe paths that feed Scenario Profiles and the Weighted Forecast, with the same approval lineage |

Two things the suite does not have are added for MAIIC. **Reserve Bank of Malawi series by file**: the policy rate and the prime lending rate are not on the World Bank; the PLR is already in the landing zone (`P2_06`) and the policy rate arrives as a small CSV through the same preview-and-commit screen, one more source tab rather than a special case. **A rule for disagreement**: a Governance Centre setting, `macro_source_precedence`, says which source wins where two overlap.

### 13.4 The Malawi series, seeded

| Code | Series | World Bank indicator | Why MAIIC needs it |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDP_GROWTH | Real GDP growth, annual % | `NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG` | The headline driver of default rates |
| CPI | Inflation, consumer prices, annual % | `FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG` | Real income of borrowers; the policy-rate path |
| MWK_USD | Official exchange rate, MWK per USD | `PA.NUS.FCRF` | Import-dependent borrowers; the industrial book |
| LENDING_RATE | Lending interest rate, % | `FR.INR.LEND` | Debt service burden; cross-check to the PLR series |
| REAL_RATE | Real interest rate, % | `FR.INR.RINR` | Affordability after inflation |
| PRIVATE_CREDIT | Domestic credit to private sector, % of GDP | `FS.AST.PRVT.GD.ZS` | Credit conditions |
| AGRI_GROWTH | Agriculture, forestry and fishing value added, annual growth % | `NV.AGR.TOTL.KD.ZG` | MAIIC's book is agricultural and agro-industrial; the harvest is its own driver |
| BROAD_MONEY | Broad money growth, annual % | `FM.LBL.BMNY.ZG` | Liquidity conditions |
| RESERVES | Total reserves in months of imports | `FI.RES.TOTL.MO` | Exchange-rate and import-cover stress |
| DEBT_GDP | Central government debt, % of GDP | `GC.DOD.TOTL.GD.ZS` | Sovereign stress and crowding out |
| CURRENT_ACCOUNT | Current account balance, % of GDP | `BN.CAB.XOKA.GD.ZS` | External balance |
| POLICY_RATE | RBM policy rate, % | by file (RBM) | The rate the PLR follows |
| PLR | Prime lending rate, % | the landing zone, `P2_06` | The floating-rate reference of the EIR engine, so the ECL and EIR modules read one series |

The IMF WEO gives the forecast years for GDP growth, inflation, the current account and government debt; the World Bank gives the actuals. A code that the World Bank later retires is a seeder change, not a code change.

### 13.5 Behaviour, stated precisely

- **Country.** `MWI` by default; the screen may fetch another country for comparison, and such rows carry their country and are never used by the FLI model.
- **Periods.** World Bank and WEO series are annual; MAIIC's FLI model runs on the frequency the series definition states. An annual value is held as the year's observation; the Weighted Forecast interpolates to quarters or months as it does today, and says so on the row.
- **Actual against forecast.** A World Bank value is an actual. A WEO value is an actual up to the estimates-start year and a forecast after it; a later WEO vintage replaces an earlier forecast and the earlier one is kept in the batch history. A forecast is never overwritten by hand without a reason.
- **Precedence** (`macro_source_precedence`, section 4.2): World Bank for actuals, IMF WEO for forecasts, the RBM file for rates; a manual entry overrides any of them only with a reason, and the override is shown on the row and in the audit log.
- **Failure.** A series the source cannot supply is reported on the preview and skipped on the command; the import never fails as a whole because one indicator is missing. A fetch that cannot reach the source after the retries says so and leaves the table as it was.
- **Provenance to the audit workbook.** The IFRS 9 impairment workbook of section 12 cites, for B5.5.49 to B5.5.54, the batch behind each series in use: source, address, fetched-at, who committed it.

### 13.6 What changes in the code

| Change | Where |
|---|---|
| `external_codes`, `country` on `macro_statistics`; `macro_source_import_batches`; `source_import_batch_id` on `macro_statistics_data` | Two migrations |
| `WorldBankFetcherService`, `ImfWeoParserService`, `SourceImportBatch`, the RBM file parser | `app/Services/Macro`, `app/Models` |
| `MacroExternalCodesSeeder` with the series of 13.4 | `database/seeders` |
| Preview and commit endpoints for the three sources; `macro.view` and `macro.manage` | `MacroStatsController`, `routes/web.php`, the permission seeder |
| `macro:import-worldbank`; a step in `eir:bootstrap`; a monthly schedule; the JSON snapshot | `app/Console/Commands`, `routes/console.php`, `docs/bootstrap/macro/` |
| The Macro Statistics screen with five tabs in the suite layout | `resources/js/Pages/FLI/MacroStats` |
| `macro_source_precedence` in the Governance Centre catalogue | `GovernanceService::catalogue()` |
| Tests: the fetcher against a recorded response, the WEO parser against a sample file, preview writes nothing, commit writes a batch, the command skips a missing series | `tests/Feature/Macro` |

Not changed: Scenario Profiles, Weighted Forecast, Credit Loss Data, Adjusted Forecast and Regression Analysis read the same tables as before; the FLI model's arithmetic is untouched.

### 13.7 Acceptance

1. Every series of 13.4 with a World Bank code previews and imports for Malawi, and the rows carry a batch with source, address and time.
2. A WEO file previews with each year marked actual or forecast, and commits with the forecast years flagged.
3. A preview writes nothing; a commit by a viewer is refused; a commit by a manager is audit-logged.
4. `macro:import-worldbank` with the network unavailable reports every series skipped and leaves the tables unchanged; `eir:bootstrap` falls back to the snapshot.
5. The Weighted Forecast and Regression screens show the same results on imported data as on the same values typed by hand.
6. The impairment workbook's forward-looking rows cite the batches in use.

### 13.8 Order of work

MS-1 the migrations, the ported services, the seeder and the command, with tests (one day); MS-2 the screen in the suite layout, with the RBM file tab (one day); MS-3 the bootstrap step, the snapshot, the schedule and the audit-workbook rows (half a day). MS-1 can start with P4b; MS-2 is the first Data Foundation screen rebuilt in the suite shape and sits with UI-2.

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 19:01:31 UTC)

Adopted and in the spec — section 13, decision D27, pushed as `7375431`. The spec is now 31 pages in the three formats.

## What section 13 records

**13.2 What MAIIC has today** — the tables (`macro_statistics`, `macro_statistics_data` with the scenario on the row, which is kept because it is ahead of the suite's design) and the six forward-looking screens; and what is missing: no external source, no preview before a write, no provenance, no command, no rule for disagreement.

**13.3 What the suite does, and is adopted** — element by element with the MAIIC mapping: indicator codes on the series (`external_codes`, `country = MWI`); `WorldBankFetcherService` and `ImfWeoParserService` ported as they are (the WEO file's UTF-16 quirk and its "Estimates Start After" column, which is where the forecast years come from); preview then commit under `macro.view` / `macro.manage`; a batch of provenance on every observation; `macro:import-worldbank` for the bootstrap and the scheduler with a committed JSON snapshot for offline installs; the five-tab screen in Data Foundation with **Scenario Assumptions** as MAIIC's governed-paths tab. Two MAIIC additions: **RBM series by file** (policy rate by CSV; the PLR read from the landing zone so ECL and EIR share one series) and **`macro_source_precedence`** as a governed setting.

**13.4 Thirteen Malawi series seeded** — GDP growth, CPI, MWK/USD, lending and real rates, private credit, **agriculture value-added growth** (MAIIC's book), broad money, reserves, debt/GDP, current account, the RBM policy rate, the PLR — each with its World Bank indicator code and why MAIIC needs it.

**13.5–13.8** — behaviour (country, annual periods, actual vs forecast and WEO vintages, precedence, non-fatal failure, provenance cited in the impairment workbook for B5.5.49–54), the code changes file by file, six acceptance checks, and MS-1 to MS-3 (two and a half days; MS-1 can start with P4b, MS-2 is the first Data Foundation screen rebuilt in the suite shape).

Also threaded: the setting in 4.2, Macro Statistics in 11.3 under Data Foundation (Macro Elements leaves the Forward-Looking sub-group), two glossary entries, and D27 in the decisions table.

The spec now carries decisions D20 to D27 and the Governance Centre has 32 settings on paper (28 in code — the four added since this morning, `ebanker_feed_route`, `loan_book_build_method`, `takeon_history_basis` and `macro_source_precedence`, go into the catalogue when the build starts).

                    ? 12  // 12-month window for Stage 1
                    : (int) round($remainingLife);  // Lifetime for Stage 2 (convert to integer months)

                // Stage 2 loan whose remaining tenor did not land exactly on
                // a generated window (understating ECL). Nearest-window keeps

                        ->first();

                if ($fliAdj) {

                    // Calculate PD after FLI adjustment

                        $stats['floored_at_zero']++;
                    } elseif ($pdPostFli > 1.0) {

                        $stats['capped_at_100']++;
                    }

                    $loan->pd_post_fli = $pdPostFli;
                    $loan->save();

                        $stats['stage_1_updated']++;
                    } else {
                        $stats['stage_2_updated']++;
                    }
                } else {

                }

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 19:06:23 UTC)

I have the full picture across the three codebases. Here is the review and what I suggest.

## How MAIIC does forward-looking adjustments today

The chain, as the code actually runs it:

1. **Regression** (`RegressionService`, `regression_models`): multiple linear regression of a credit-loss proxy (a `macro_credit_loss_definitions` series — observed default rate, NPL ratio or similar) on one or more macro series, aligned by period; stores coefficients, R², adjusted R², train window; a model can be *approved* for use.
2. **Parameters per reporting period** (`fli_reporting_periods_parameters`): for a scenario set, the chosen macro statistic, the PD proxy, the base period's macro value and proxy value, and a **single slope and intercept** — one macro variable only.
3. **Forecast windows** (`fli_adj`): for each window (0, 1, 2 … periods ahead) the *scenario-weighted* macro value is typed or fetched; `predicted = slope × macro + intercept`; **`fli_adj = predicted / predicted(window 0) − 1`** — a relative uplift against the base period.
4. **Apply to loans** (`ExternalCalculationsController::applyToLoans`): Stage 3 → PD 100%; Stage 1 → the 12-month window; Stage 2 → the window nearest the remaining tenor; **`pd_post_fli = pd_prefli × (1 + fli_adj)`**, floored at 0 and capped at 1.
5. **ECL** reads `pd_post_fli` (`TimePhasedEclService`, `RecalculateEcl --pd=pd_post_fli`); the ECL recompute is forbidden from writing `pd_post_fli` back — the FLI engine owns it.

So the post-FLI PD *is* already what drives the ECL, and the sequencing is right. The weaknesses are real, though:

- **One macro variable per period.** The multiple regression is trained, but the parameter table carries only `regression_slope` / `regression_intercept`, so the applied model is univariate even when the approved model is not.
- **No sign or strength test.** The model can be approved with a negative R² sign that contradicts economics; nothing checks it.
- **No lags, no transforms.** GDP growth this quarter is regressed on defaults this quarter; the plain-PHP and FDH apps both know the link is usually lagged.
- **No manual route.** The only way to a `pd_post_fli` is through the regression. There is no screen where Finance can say "this quarter, +15 percent on Stage 2 agriculture, because of the drought, approved by X" — which is what actually happens in a small institution, and what IFRS 9 B5.5.52 contemplates as an overlay.
- **No correlation finder.** The analyst must already know which macro series to regress on.
- **No lineage on the loan.** `fli_adj` on the loan row says the number, not which parameter set, model version and scenario produced it.

## What the two FDH apps add

The **plain-PHP app** has the governed *correlation test*: each regression definition carries the expected sign (positive or negative) and an **R² cut-off**; the calculator computes r and R² and marks the pair red/green — failed sign, failed cut-off, weak, passed. Simple and auditable.

The **FDH Laravel app** turns that into **Auto-Correlate** (`CorrelationFinder`): sweeps every macro series × every credit-loss proxy × a governed **lag grid**, computes Spearman and Theil-Sen first (robust), then Pearson and a one-variable OLS, ranks each pair by a composite score, and saves the ranked suggestions with a plain-language reason under an immutable analysis run with an input hash. Fail-closed: too little overlap is rejected with the reason, never fabricated.

## What I suggest for MAIIC (five pieces)

| # | Piece | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Correlation Finder** (Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking Model) | Port FDH's `CorrelationFinder`: X = every active macro series (now fed from section 13), Y = every credit-loss proxy MAIIC holds (observed default rate by product group, NPL ratio, roll rates from the transition matrices), lag grid governed (0, 3, 6, 9, 12 months), transforms (level, change, log-change), Spearman + Pearson + OLS, ranked suggestions with reasons, saved as an immutable run. The plain-PHP tests become governed thresholds: expected sign per pair and an R² cut-off, both in the Governance Centre. |
| 2 | **Regression that applies what it trained** | The parameter table stores the **approved model id** and its coefficient vector, not one slope; `predicted` uses all its variables; the model must have passed the sign and cut-off tests to be approvable; maker-checker on approval (it already has `is_approved`, without a second person). |
| 3 | **Three FLI routes, one governed choice** | A setting, `fli_adjustment_route`: **Regression** (today's chain, repaired); **Manual overlay** — a new screen where a reviewer enters `fli_adj` per scenario, window and, optionally, product group or stage, with a reason and an attachment, approved by a second person; **Regression plus overlay** — the regression result then a manual adjustment on top, each shown separately on the loan. All three write the same `fli_adj` rows, so step 4 and the ECL do not change. |
| 4 | **Lineage on the loan** | `fli_source` (regression / manual / both), `fli_parameter_id`, `fli_model_version`, `scenario_set_id` on the loan-book row, so the ECL report and the impairment audit workbook can say for every loan which model, which overlay and which approval produced its post-FLI PD. |
| 5 | **Scenario weighting made visible** | The weighted macro value of step 3 is today a typed number; with section 13's base/mild/severe paths and the scenario-set probabilities it becomes computed and shown — the row says 40% base, 30% mild, 30% severe and the three values behind the weight. |

The arithmetic of steps 4 and 5 stays as it is: `pd_post_fli = pd_prefli × (1 + fli_adj)`, floored and capped, Stage 3 at 100%, Stage 1 at the 12-month window and Stage 2 at the lifetime window. That part is sound and already tested.

Where it sits in the layout: Correlation Finder, Regression Analysis, FLI Adjustments (the three routes) and Weighted Forecast under **Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking Model**; the macro series and scenario assumptions under **Data Foundation › Macro Statistics** (section 13); the thresholds, the route and the approvals in the **Governance Centre**; the finder's runs and the overlays in the impairment audit workbook.

Effort: about four days — one for the finder port, one for the regression repair, one for the manual-overlay screen and the route setting, one for lineage, tests and the workbook rows.

If you agree, it goes into the spec as section 14 (glossary to 15), with the three new settings (`fli_adjustment_route`, `fli_expected_sign_test`, `fli_r2_cutoff`) in 4.2 and the screens in 11.3.

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 19:08:16 UTC)

Short version: MAIIC has the pieces of scenario handling but not the governance, and it weights at the wrong point. Here is what the code shows, what good practice asks for, and how to get there.

## What MAIIC has today

Two overlapping structures that are not linked: `scenario_profiles` with child scenarios (name, probability, `is_base_case`, a JSON blob of paths), used by the Weighted Forecast; and `scenario_sets` + `scenario_probabilities` (name, probability, order), used by the FLI parameters. Neither carries a reporting period, a version, a narrative, a source vintage, an approval or a lock. Paths are typed into the profile. And the method weights the **macro value** across scenarios and then runs one regression on the weighted value — so the probability-weighted ECL is never actually computed; what is computed is the ECL at the weighted macro, which ignores non-linearity (the downside hurts more than the upside helps).

## What best practice asks for

| Principle | Source | What it means in practice |
|---|---|---|
| Unbiased, probability-weighted, a range of outcomes | IFRS 9 5.5.17(a), B5.5.42 | At least a base, an upside and a downside with weights that sum to 100; the ECL is the weighted average of the ECL under each scenario, not the ECL at an average scenario |
| Reasonable and supportable, without undue cost | B5.5.49–54 | Paths from published sources (IMF WEO, World Bank, RBM), with the vintage recorded; judgement documented where sources end |
| Scenarios and weights are governed | Basel GCRAECL principles 2 and 5; auditors' expectation | Approved by two people (Finance and Risk), locked with the period's ECL, changed only by a new version with a reason, reviewed at least annually |
| Severity calibrated, not invented | Common practice | The downside is anchored to what Malawi has actually lived through: the 2023 devaluation (44%), the 2016 drought, the 2012 float; the set says which history it is calibrated to |
| One house view | GCRAECL; audit consistency | The same scenario set drives the ECL, the sensitivity disclosures, the stress test and the budget; a different set for each is a finding |
| Disclosed | IFRS 7.35G | The narratives, the weights, the key paths per scenario, the ECL under each scenario and under 100% weight on each, and the sensitivity to the weights |
| Overlays are governed, not hidden | GCRAECL; B5.5.52 | A management overlay sits on an approved set, with a reason, an owner, an expiry and a second approval; shown separately in the ECL |
| Back-tested | Model risk practice | Each period, the previous set's base path is compared with what happened, and the realised default rate with the predicted; outside the range triggers a review of the weights |

## What to build (section 15 if you agree)

1. **One governed object: the Scenario Set per reporting period.** The two existing structures merge into it (a migration maps what is there): period, name, version, status (draft → proposed → approved → locked), narrative, source vintage (for example "IMF WEO April 2026, World Bank 2025 actuals, RBM MPC March 2026"), proposed-by, approved-by, locked-at. Under it, three or more **scenarios** with probability weights that must sum to 100, a narrative each, and the **paths**: per macro series per horizon, the base path from section 13's sources and the other scenarios as governed **shocks** on it (percent change, absolute, replace, multiplier, by year offset — the ZNBS shock model), so a downside is an auditable transformation of the base, not a second set of typed numbers.
2. **Weight the ECL, not the macro.** A setting, `scenario_weighting_method`: *Weight the ECL across scenarios* (recommended: PD under each scenario, ECL under each, weighted sum) or *Weight the macro path, one ECL* (today's method, kept for reconciliation to past results). The FLI chain of the last message runs once per scenario under the first option; the loan row carries the ECL per scenario and the weighted figure.
3. **Governance rules as settings**, in the Governance Centre: minimum number of scenarios (3), a floor on the base weight (say 40 percent) and a ceiling on any single weight, the calibration note required on every downside, the annual review date, and the rule that an overlay needs an approved set.
4. **Overlay register.** Manual FLI overlays (the manual route of the last message) live in a register tied to the scenario set: amount or percent, scope (portfolio, product group, stage), reason, evidence attachment, owner, expiry date, two approvals; shown as their own line in the ECL and the disclosure.
5. **Back-test and sensitivity, computed every period**: previous base path vs actuals per macro series; predicted vs realised default rate; ECL under each scenario and under 100% weights; ECL sensitivity to ±10 points on the weights. Stored with the set, so IFRS 7.35G is a report, not a spreadsheet.
6. **Where it lives**: Governance Centre › **Scenario Sets** (create, propose, approve, lock, versions, history); Data Foundation › Macro Statistics › Scenario Assumptions (the paths and shocks); Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking › FLI Adjustments (apply per scenario); Report Hub › IFRS 9 Disclosure (the 7.35G tables) and the impairment audit workbook (one row per principle above, citing the set).

For MAIIC specifically, I would seed the first set with base = WEO, upside = base shocked by the 2021–22 recovery, downside = base shocked by the 2023 devaluation year, severe = the 2016 drought plus devaluation, weights 50/15/25/10 as a starting proposal for Dr Thom — all four shocks are documented Malawi history, which is the strongest answer to "why these".

Effort: three days for the set, scenarios, shocks and governance; one for the ECL-per-scenario run; one for the back-test, sensitivity and disclosure tables. Say so and it goes into the spec as section 15 (the FLI piece as 14), with the settings in 4.2 and the screens in 11.3.

## 14. Forward-looking adjustments: the regression, the correlation finder and the manual route

### 14.1 In plain language

A probability of default measured from MAIIC's own history says how often borrowers like this one have defaulted in the past. IFRS 9 asks for something more: the probability that applies to the economy that is coming, not the one that has been. The "forward-looking adjustment" is the step that turns the historical probability (the pre-FLI PD) into the one the expected credit loss is calculated on (the post-FLI PD). MAIIC's system already does this, and does it in the right order: the adjustment is worked out from a regression of credit losses on the economy, applied to each loan's PD, and the ECL reads the adjusted figure. What is missing is the discipline around it: a way to find which economic series actually explains MAIIC's losses, a test that the relationship makes economic sense before it is used, a way for Finance to apply an adjustment by judgement when the statistics cannot, and a record on each loan of where its adjustment came from. Decision D28 adds those four things and changes none of the arithmetic that already works.

### 14.2 How the adjustment works today

The chain, as the code runs it:

| Step | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A **regression** relates a credit-loss proxy (an observed default rate, an NPL ratio) to one or more macro series over a training window; the model stores its coefficients, R-squared and window, and can be marked approved | `RegressionService`, `regression_models` |
| 2 | For a reporting period and a scenario set, a **parameter record** names the macro statistic, the PD proxy, the base period's values and a single slope and intercept | `fli_reporting_periods_parameters` |
| 3 | For each **forecast window** (0, 1, 2 … periods ahead) the scenario-weighted macro value is entered; the predicted proxy is slope × value + intercept; the **adjustment** is the predicted value divided by the base window's predicted value, less one: a relative uplift on the base period | `fli_adj` |
| 4 | **Applied to loans**: Stage 3 is set to 100 percent; Stage 1 takes the 12-month window; Stage 2 takes the window nearest its remaining life; post-FLI PD = pre-FLI PD × (1 + adjustment), floored at 0 and capped at 100 percent | `ExternalCalculationsController::applyToLoans` |
| 5 | The **ECL** reads the post-FLI PD; the ECL recalculation is forbidden from writing it back, because the FLI engine owns it | `TimePhasedEclService`, `RecalculateEcl --pd=pd_post_fli` |

Steps 4 and 5 are sound and tested and are kept exactly as they are. The weaknesses are in steps 1 to 3:

- **One variable is applied even when several were trained.** The parameter record holds one slope and one intercept, so the model that reaches the loans is univariate whatever the approved model was.
- **No test of sense.** A model can be approved whose coefficient has the wrong sign (losses falling as unemployment rises) or whose R-squared is negligible; nothing stops it.
- **No lags, no transforms.** The economy of this quarter is regressed on the losses of this quarter; the link is usually lagged, and often in changes rather than levels.
- **Only one road.** The only way to a post-FLI PD is the regression. There is no screen on which Finance can say "for this quarter, plus fifteen percent on Stage 2 agriculture, because of the drought, approved by two people", which is what a small institution actually needs and what B5.5.52 contemplates.
- **No finder.** The analyst must already know which series to regress on.
- **No lineage on the loan.** The loan row holds the number, not which model, parameter set and scenario produced it.

### 14.3 The correlation finder

The finder answers the first question an analyst has: which economic series, at what lag, in what form, explains MAIIC's losses, and how well. It is the Dupleix suite's "auto-correlate", ported.

- **The sweep.** Every active macro series (section 13) against every credit-loss proxy MAIIC holds (observed default rate by product group, NPL ratio, the roll rates behind the transition matrices), across a governed lag grid (0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months) and three transforms (level, change, change in logarithm). For each combination it computes a rank correlation first (Spearman, which is robust to the odd year) and a robust slope (Theil-Sen), then Pearson's r and a one-variable least-squares fit.
- **The ranking.** Each pair is scored on strength, sign agreement with what economics expects, overlap length and whether the series can be forecast (a series no source projects cannot drive a forward-looking adjustment, and is ranked down for it). One suggestion per pair at its best lag, with a plain-language reason: "Agriculture value added, lagged two quarters, change: Spearman −0.71 over 28 quarters; sign as expected; forecastable from the IMF".
- **Fail-closed.** A pair with too little overlap is rejected with the reason, never fabricated; a sweep with no proxy data produces no suggestions and says so.
- **Immutable runs.** Every sweep is an analysis run with the hash of the inputs it read, so a suggestion can be reproduced from the data vintage; a later sweep is a new run, not an edit.
- **The tests, governed.** Two thresholds from the Governance Centre decide what may go forward: the **expected sign** per pair (positive, negative or not stated) and an **R-squared cut-off**. A pair that fails either is shown in red with the reason, as the earlier Dupleix calculator did it; it may still be studied, but it cannot be approved as a model.

### 14.4 The regression, repaired

- **The model that is trained is the model that is applied.** The parameter record stores the approved model's id and its full coefficient vector; the predicted proxy uses every variable in it, each at its own lag and transform.
- **Approval needs the tests and two people.** A model may be approved only if it passes the sign and cut-off tests of 14.3, and approval is maker-checker: the person who trained it cannot approve it. An approved model is versioned; a retrained model is a new version and the old one stays attached to the periods that used it.
- **Back-test on the row.** Each period, the model's predicted proxy for the period just ended is compared with the realised proxy and the difference stored, so a model that has stopped working is visible before it is reused.

### 14.5 Three routes to the adjustment, one governed choice

A Governance Centre setting, `fli_adjustment_route`, says how the adjustment is produced for a period. All three routes write the same adjustment rows, so steps 4 and 5 of 14.2 do not change.

| Route | What it is | When it is the right one |
|---|---|---|
| **Regression** (seeded default) | The chain of 14.2 with the repairs of 14.4: the approved model, the scenario paths of section 15, the predicted proxy per window, the relative uplift | When an approved model exists and passes its back-test |
| **Manual overlay** | A screen on which a reviewer enters the adjustment per scenario and window and, optionally, per product group or stage, with a reason and an attachment; a second person approves; the overlay has an owner and an expiry date | When no model is approvable, or when an event the statistics cannot see (a drought, a devaluation, a policy change) has to be reflected now |
| **Regression plus overlay** | The regression result, then a manual adjustment on top; each shown separately on the loan and in the ECL | When the model is sound but judgement says it is not enough |

The manual overlay is a register, not a free field: every entry carries its scope, reason, evidence, owner, expiry, proposer and approver, and the ECL shows the overlay as its own line, which is how the auditor and the Board see what judgement added.

### 14.6 Lineage on the loan

Four columns are added to the loan-book row beside the adjustment and the post-FLI PD: the route used, the parameter record, the model version and the scenario set. The ECL report and the impairment audit workbook can then say, for every loan, which model, which overlay, which scenario and which approval produced its post-FLI PD. The scenario-weighted macro value of step 3, typed today, becomes computed and shown: the row says which scenarios, at which weights, gave the figure, and the three values behind it.

### 14.7 Where it lives, and the settings

Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking Model: **Correlation Finder** (new), **Regression Analysis** (repaired), **FLI Adjustments** (new: the route, the regression result, the overlay register, the apply-to-loans step with its counts), **Weighted Forecast** (now computed from the scenario set). The three settings in the Governance Centre (section 4.2): `fli_adjustment_route` (seeded: Regression), `fli_expected_sign_test` (seeded: Required), `fli_r2_cutoff` (seeded: 30 percent, a common starting threshold for annual macro data; MAIIC may tighten it). The finder's runs, the approved models and the overlays are cited in the impairment audit workbook's rows for B5.5.49 to B5.5.54.

### 14.8 Acceptance and order of work

1. The finder sweeps every series and proxy and ranks suggestions with reasons; a pair with fewer than the governed minimum of overlapping periods is rejected with the reason.
2. A model that fails the sign or cut-off test cannot be approved; approval needs a second person; the applied prediction uses every coefficient of the approved model.
3. Each route produces adjustment rows; the loans' post-FLI PDs equal pre-FLI × (1 + adjustment), floored and capped, Stage 3 at 100 percent, as today.
4. Every loan row names its route, parameter record, model version and scenario set; the ECL shows the overlay as its own line.
5. The existing ECL tests pass unchanged on the regression route.

FL-1 the finder (one day); FL-2 the regression repair with its tests (one day); FL-3 the FLI Adjustments screen, the overlay register and the route setting (one day); FL-4 lineage, the computed weighting, the back-test and the workbook rows (one day). FL-1 needs the macro series of section 13; the rest can follow P4b.

## 15. Economic scenarios: governance and incorporation

### 15.1 In plain language

The forward-looking adjustment depends on what the economy is assumed to do. IFRS 9 does not let that be one guess: it asks for an unbiased, probability-weighted view across a range of possible outcomes (5.5.17(a), B5.5.42). In practice that means a base view, a better one and a worse one, each with a story, a set of figures and a weight, agreed by the people accountable for it and kept once the period's numbers are struck. MAIIC's system holds scenarios today, but in two unconnected places, without a period, a version, a narrative, a source, an approval or a lock, and it uses them at the wrong point: it averages the economy and calculates one loss, where the standard asks for the loss under each economy, then the average. Decision D29 makes the scenario set a governed object and moves the weighting to where it belongs.

### 15.2 What good practice asks for

| Principle | Where it comes from | What it means for MAIIC |
|---|---|---|
| Unbiased and probability-weighted, over a range of outcomes | IFRS 9 5.5.17(a), B5.5.42 | At least a base, an upside and a downside, with weights that sum to 100; the ECL is the weighted average of the ECL under each scenario, not the ECL at the average economy |
| Reasonable and supportable, without undue cost or effort | B5.5.49 to B5.5.54 | Paths from published sources (the IMF World Economic Outlook, the World Bank, the Reserve Bank of Malawi), with the vintage recorded; judgement written down where the sources stop |
| Governed | The Basel Committee's guidance on credit risk and accounting for expected credit losses, principles 2 and 5; the auditors' expectation | Approved by two people, one from Finance and one from Risk; locked with the period's ECL; changed only by a new version with a reason; reviewed at least once a year |
| Severity calibrated to history | Common practice | The downside is anchored to what Malawi has lived through: the 2023 devaluation, the 2016 drought, the 2012 float; the set says which history each scenario is calibrated to |
| One house view | Basel guidance; audit consistency | The same scenario set drives the ECL, the sensitivity disclosures, the stress test and the budget; a different set for each is a finding |
| Disclosed | IFRS 7.35G | The narratives, the weights, the key paths per scenario, the ECL under each scenario and with 100 percent weight on each, and the sensitivity to the weights |
| Overlays governed, not hidden | Basel guidance; B5.5.52 | A management overlay sits on an approved set, with a reason, an owner, an expiry and a second approval, and is shown separately |
| Back-tested | Model-risk practice | Each period the previous set's base path is compared with what happened, and the predicted default rate with the realised; a miss outside the range triggers a review of the weights |

### 15.3 The scenario set, as a governed object

The two existing structures (`scenario_profiles` with its child scenarios, and `scenario_sets` with `scenario_probabilities`) become one, and a migration maps what is there.

**The set**, one per reporting period: period; name; version; status (draft, proposed, approved, locked); the narrative; the source vintage ("IMF WEO April 2026; World Bank 2025 actuals; RBM Monetary Policy Committee, March 2026"); proposed by; approved by (two people); locked at. A set is locked when the period's ECL is locked; a change after that is a new version with a reason, and the locked version stays attached to the period.

**The scenarios** under it, three or more: name; probability weight (the weights must sum to 100); the narrative; the calibration note that says which history the scenario is anchored to; and the **paths**: for each macro series and each horizon, the base scenario's path comes from the sources of section 13, and every other scenario is expressed as a governed **shock** on the base, by series and year offset, of one of four kinds: a percentage change, an absolute change, a replacement value, or a multiplier. A downside is therefore an auditable transformation of the base, not a second set of typed numbers; change the base and the shocked paths follow.

### 15.4 Weighting the loss, not the economy

A Governance Centre setting, `scenario_weighting_method`, with two options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Weight the ECL across scenarios** (seeded) | The forward-looking chain of section 14 runs once per scenario; each loan carries a PD and an ECL under each scenario; the reported ECL is the probability-weighted sum. This captures non-linearity: a downside hurts more than an upside helps, and the average of the losses is higher than the loss at the average |
| Weight the macro path, one ECL | Today's method: the scenario-weighted macro value, one regression, one ECL. Kept so that past periods can be reproduced and the two methods reconciled when the switch is made |

Switching is a governed change with an effective date; the first period run under the new method shows both figures and the difference, which is itself a disclosure the auditors will want.

### 15.5 The rules, as settings

In the Governance Centre: the minimum number of scenarios (seeded 3); a floor on the base scenario's weight (seeded 40 percent) and a ceiling on any single weight (seeded 60 percent); whether a calibration note is required on every downside (seeded Required); the annual review month; and the rule that an overlay needs an approved set (seeded Required). Each is changed under maker-checker with a reason, like every other setting.

### 15.6 Overlays, back-tests and sensitivity

- **The overlay register** of section 14.5 is tied to the scenario set: an overlay names the set it sits on, and a set cannot be locked with an unapproved overlay against it. Each overlay is shown as its own line in the ECL and in the disclosure.
- **Back-test, every period**: for each macro series, the previous set's base path against the actual now known; for each proxy, the predicted default rate against the realised. The results are stored with the set, and a miss outside the scenario range raises a flag that the weights are to be reviewed before the next set is proposed.
- **Sensitivity, every period**: the ECL under each scenario; the ECL with 100 percent weight on each; the ECL with ten points moved from the base to the downside and to the upside. Stored with the set, so the IFRS 7.35G tables are a report from the system, not a spreadsheet beside it.

### 15.7 The first set, proposed

For MAIIC the first set is seeded as a proposal for Dr Thom, every scenario anchored to a year Malawi has lived through:

| Scenario | Weight | Anchored to |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 50 | The IMF World Economic Outlook path, World Bank actuals, the RBM's stated policy path |
| Upside | 15 | The 2021 to 2022 recovery: growth and the harvest above the base, inflation below |
| Downside | 25 | The 2023 devaluation year: the kwacha down by 44 percent, inflation and lending rates up |
| Severe | 10 | The 2016 drought together with a devaluation: the harvest fails and the currency falls |

The weights are a starting point and are his to set; the anchors are the answer to the question "why these".

### 15.8 Where it lives

Governance Centre › **Scenario Sets** (create, propose, approve, lock, versions, history, the back-test and sensitivity stored with each); Data Foundation › Macro Statistics › **Scenario Assumptions** (the base paths and the shocks); Financial Modelling › Forward-Looking Model › **FLI Adjustments** (the chain run per scenario); Report Hub › **IFRS 9 Disclosure** (the 7.35G tables) and the impairment audit workbook, which carries one row per principle of 15.2 citing the set in force.

### 15.9 Acceptance and order of work

1. A set cannot be proposed with weights that do not sum to 100, fewer scenarios than the minimum, or a downside without its calibration note; it cannot be approved by its proposer; it cannot be changed after lock except as a new version with a reason.
2. Every non-base path equals the base path transformed by its recorded shocks, and changing the base re-derives them.
3. Under the seeded weighting method, every loan carries a PD and an ECL per scenario and the reported ECL is the weighted sum; under the other method the figure equals today's.
4. The back-test and the sensitivity tables are produced for a locked period and agree with a hand calculation on a sample.
5. The disclosure report prints the narratives, weights, paths, per-scenario ECL and weight sensitivity of the set in force.

SC-1 the set, the scenarios, the shocks, the migration from the two old structures and the governance rules (two days); SC-2 the ECL per scenario and the weighting method (one day); SC-3 the overlay tie, the back-test, the sensitivity and the disclosure tables (one day); SC-4 the first set seeded as a proposal (half a day). SC-1 follows section 13; SC-2 follows FL-3.

## Section 14 — Forward-looking adjustments

- **14.1 Background** — why the economy enters the loss estimate: ECL = PD × LGD × EAD discounted at the EIR; the PD from MAIIC's transition matrices is a through-the-cycle average and IFRS 9 wants a point-in-time figure (5.5.17(c), B5.5.49); what a regression does, and the three things that matter in practice — lags, changes rather than levels, economic sense; and where judgement is allowed (B5.5.52).
- **14.2 In plain language** and **14.3 How it works today** — the five-step chain as the code runs it (regression → parameter record → windows and the relative uplift → applied to loans with the stage rules, floored and capped → ECL reads post-FLI), with steps 4–5 declared sound and kept, and the six weaknesses named.
- **14.4 The correlation finder** — the sweep over series × proxies × lag grid × transforms, Spearman and Theil-Sen first, ranking with plain-language reasons, fail-closed, immutable runs with input hashes, and the plain-PHP sign and R² tests as governed thresholds.
- **14.5 The regression, repaired** — the full coefficient vector applied, approval only after the tests and by a second person, versioned models, a back-test on the row.
- **14.6 Three routes** — Regression (seeded), Manual overlay (a register with scope, reason, evidence, owner, expiry, two approvals, shown as its own line), Regression plus overlay; one setting, same adjustment rows, steps 4–5 untouched.
- **14.7 Lineage on the loan**, **14.8 Where it lives and the settings**, **14.9 Acceptance and FL-1 to FL-4** (four days).

## Section 15 — Economic scenarios

- **15.1 Background** — what a scenario is; why one path understates the loss (non-linearity); why ECL scenarios are not stress tests though they share economics; why the weights draw scrutiny and the three disciplines that answer it; Malawi's own anchors (2023 devaluation, 2016 drought, 2012 float, 2021–22 recovery).
- **15.2–15.3** — in plain language, and the eight principles with their sources (IFRS 9 B5.5.42, B5.5.49–54; Basel GCRAECL principles 2 and 5; IFRS 7.35G).
- **15.4 The scenario set as a governed object** — one per period: version, status draft→proposed→approved→locked, narrative, source vintage, two approvals; scenarios with weights summing to 100, calibration notes, and paths as governed **shocks** on the base (percent, absolute, replace, multiplier, by series and year); the two old structures merged.
- **15.5 Weighting the loss, not the economy** — `scenario_weighting_method`, seeded to weight the ECL across scenarios; the old method kept for reconciliation; the switch period shows both.
- **15.6 Rules as settings**, **15.7 overlays tied to the set, back-tests and sensitivity stored each period** (the 7.35G tables as a report), **15.8 the first set proposed** (Base 50 / Upside 15 / Downside 25 / Severe 10, each anchored to a Malawi year), **15.9 where it lives**, **15.10 acceptance and SC-1 to SC-4** (four and a half days).

Threaded through: **D28** and **D29** in the decisions table; eight new settings in 4.2 (route, sign test, R² cut-off, weighting method, minimum scenarios, weight bounds, calibration note, overlay-needs-approved-set); the screens in 11.3 (Correlation Finder, FLI Adjustments and Scenario Sets as new; Scenario Profiles retired into Scenario Sets under Governance); five glossary entries.

def sha(p):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(p, "rb") as f:
        for b in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""): h.update(b)
    return h.hexdigest()
def head(repo):
    try: return subprocess.check_output(["git", "-C", SRC[repo], "rev-parse", "HEAD"], text=True).strip()
    except Exception: return "not a git repository"

if os.path.isdir(DST): shutil.rmtree(DST)
entries = []; missing = []
for repo, path, section, what in FILES:
    src = os.path.join(SRC[repo], *path.split("/"))
    if not os.path.isfile(src): missing.append((repo, path)); continue
    dst = os.path.join(DST, repo, *path.split("/")); os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dst), exist_ok=True); shutil.copyfile(src, dst)
    entries.append({"repo": repo, "path": path, "spec_section": section, "verify": what, "sha256": sha(dst), "bytes": os.path.getsize(dst)})
manifest = {"purpose": "Reference logic the specification cites, copied verbatim from Dupleix's own repositories so that the completeness of spec v4 can be verified against working code. Code only; no client data.",
            "assembled": datetime.date.today().isoformat(),
            "sources": {k: {"path": v, "commit": head(k)} for k, v in SRC.items()}, "files": entries}
json.dump(manifest, open(os.path.join(DST, "manifest.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8"), indent=2)
by = {}
for e in entries:
    for sec in [x.strip() for x in e["spec_section"].split(",")]:
        by.setdefault(sec, []).append(e)
def key(sec):
    parts = sec.replace("section ", "").split()[0].split(".")
    return tuple(int(x) if x.isdigit() else 0 for x in parts)
lines = ["# Reference logic for verifying spec v4", "",
         "Verbatim copies of the files the specification (`docs/MAIIC_EIR_Engine_Specification_v4_2026-10-07.md`) cites as the source of a design, taken from Dupleix's own repositories at the commits in `manifest.json`. They are here so that a reviewer can check each section of the specification against the code it was written from, and so that the build can port rather than reinvent. Code only: no client data, no logos, no documents of another client.", "",
         "| Source | Repository | Commit |", "|---|---|---|"]
for k, v in manifest["sources"].items(): lines.append(f"| `{k}` | `{v['path']}` | `{v['commit'][:12]}` |")
lines += ["", "## By specification section", ""]
for sec in sorted(by, key=key):
    lines.append(f"### Section {sec}"); lines.append(""); lines.append("| File | What to verify |"); lines.append("|---|---|")
    for e in by[sec]: lines.append(f"| `{e['repo']}/{e['path']}` | {e['verify']} |")
    lines.append("")
open(os.path.join(DST, "README.md"), "w", encoding="utf-8").write("\n".join(lines))
print(len(entries), "files copied;", round(sum(e["bytes"] for e in entries)/1e6, 2), "MB; missing:", missing)

## `docs/reference/` in the MAICC repo

63 files copied verbatim from the three source repositories, pinned to their commits in `manifest.json` (ZNBS suite `5be6d97a`, FDH Laravel `98de97db`, plain-PHP FDH `09e8e726`), each with a SHA-256, the spec section it supports and one line on what to verify. `README.md` indexes them by section:

| Spec section | What is there to verify against |
|---|---|
| **6** Ingestion and bootstrap | `IcaapBootstrapCommand`, `SourceImportBatch`, the import-manifest migration, a committed-input import command |
| **11** The suite UI | `nav.js`, `AppLayout.vue`, `Sidebar`, `Topbar`, `Icon`, `StatCard`, `EmptyState`, `useTheme.js`, the no-flash `app.blade.php`, `tailwind.config.js`, the help panel and button, `SCOPING_NOTES.md` (the grouping convention) |
| **12** Audit workbooks and trace | `audit_workbook.py`, `build_audit.py`, `md_to_pdf.py`, the directive registry and one example module (shape only), `Audit/Trace.vue`, `Audit/Index.vue` |
| **13** Macro statistics | `WorldBankFetcherService`, `ImfWeoParserService`, `ImportWorldBankMacroCommand`, `MacroExternalCodesSeeder`, `MacroController`, the three models, the two migrations, `Macro/Index.vue` |
| **14** Forward-looking | the whole `app/Services/Fli/` set (`CorrelationFinder`, `RegressionEngine`, `Diagnostics`, `Guardrail`, `AdjustmentMethodEngine`, `CreditLossProxyDeriver`, `FliSeriesProfiler`, `StatisticsSidecar`, `StructuralEventsRegister`, `ScenarioWeightValidator`, `MacroModule`), `CalculatorController`, `Calculators/Fli.vue`, `Governance/FliRegisters.vue`; and from the plain-PHP app the regression calculator, definitions and fetches with the original sign and R² tests |
| **15** Scenarios | the scenarios, shocks, engine-extension, governance and parameter-library migrations, `ScenarioController`, `ScenarioSupportingDocumentController`, `ApprovalAuditLog`, and the governed-assumptions tab in `Macro/Index.vue` |

Code only — no client data, documents or logos. Eighteen of the files mention their origin in comments, which is right for a reference folder and is why section 0 of the spec now says: the designs of sections 6 and 11–15 are taken from the Dupleix suite, the code is under `docs/reference/` indexed by section and pinned to source commits, so the specification's completeness can be verified against working code and the build can port rather than reinvent.

One thing the folder also makes visible: FDH's `Fli/` set is richer than what section 14 describes (a structural-events register, a proxy deriver, a series profiler, guardrails). Section 14 covers the finder, the regression and the routes; if you want the events register and guardrails named explicitly as adoptions, that is a short addition.

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 19:19:01 UTC)

Taking "the app" as MAICC-IFRS9 (the one the spec is for), here are the engines it has, grouped the way the suite layout will present them. Each is a real service or job on the branch, not a screen label.

## Financial Modelling — the ECL engines

| Engine | What it computes | Where in code |
|---|---|---|
| **Staging / SICR** | DPD staging waterfall from the five arrears buckets against governed thresholds; SICR groups, items and triggers; qualitative overrides (`ifrs9stage_pre/post_qualitative`) | `StagingClassifier`, the SICR controllers, `StageingRulesController` |
| **PD — transition matrices** | Monthly transition profiles between internal grades, cumulative matrices, PD per grade and horizon | `TransitionMatrixService`, `TransitionMatrixCummulativeService`, the three TransitionMatrix controllers |
| **LGD** | Loss given default from payment tracking (chunked, queued): recoveries, cures, discounted payments, collateral allocation; monthly and cumulative LGD | `CalculateLGDJob`, `ProcessLGDChunkJob`, `ProcessLGDPayments`, `CalculateDiscountingJob`, `LGDCalculationController` |
| **Forward-looking (FLI)** | Multiple linear regression of a loss proxy on macro series; scenario-weighted forecast; adjustment per window; applied to PDs (`pd_post_fli`) | `RegressionService`, `MacroForecastWeightedService`, `ExternalCalculationsController` |
| **ECL** | PD × LGD × EAD per stage; horizon-proxy discounting (Stage 1 capped at one year); the **time-phased, scenario-weighted ECL discounted at the EIR** | `EclDiscountingService`, `EclDiscountRateService`, `TimePhasedEclService`, `RecalculateEcl` |

## Financial Modelling — the EIR engine (the branch's subject)

| Engine | What it computes | Where in code |
|---|---|---|
| **Contractual interest** | What E-Banker posts: prior month-end balance × rate × days / 365, drawdown month from the disbursement day, moratorium compounding monthly, quarterly periods compounded | `ContractualInterestService` |
| **Schedule generator** | Version 1 expected cash flows on actual dates: both moratorium shapes, grace, EMI types, sanction-vs-balance basis; draft → approved workflow | `ScheduleGeneratorService`, `ScheduleWorkflowService` |
| **EIR solver** | The rate that discounts the expected flows to the net amount advanced, on actual dates under the governed day count; readiness blockers; reopening archived to history | `EirCalculationService`, `CalculateEirService`, `CalculateEirJob`, `EirReadinessService`, `EirCoverageService` |
| **Revenue recognition** | Interest at the EIR on amortised cost per period; fee amortisation under the 25-rule fee rulebook; the revenue shift vs contractual | `EirRevenueService`, `RunEirRevenueJob`, `FeeRuleMatcher` |
| **Spread derivation** | Margin over PLR from the loan books, with drift flagged | `SpreadDerivationService` |
| **GL reconciliation** | Ledger vs contractual vs EIR with eight named causes; the three-term variance bridge to the TB (YTD rule applied on read) | `EirGlReconciliationService`, `TrialBalanceMovementService` |

Not yet built on the EIR side: floating-rate resets (P5), arrears re-estimation (P6), restructuring/modification (P7), the as-at-any-date view (6.11).

## Risk & Regulatory / Monitoring

| Engine | What it computes | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Stress testing** | Per-stage PD multipliers and LGD add-ons recomputed loan by loan (a port of the FDH methodology, done properly rather than scaling an aggregate) | `StressTestingController` |
| **Sensitivity, EWS, data quality, RBM classification, IFRS 9 vs RBM, concentration** | Report-side engines inside the IFRS 9 hub (30 reports) | `Ifrs9ReportsController` |

## Governance

| Engine | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Governance Centre** | 28 governed conventions in code (40 on paper after today), maker-checker, effective dates, resolution by date |
| **Audit logger** | Old/new values on every governed change |

## Not in MAIIC (and in the ZNBS suite, for comparison)

Capital/RWA, liquidity (LCR/NSFR), IRRBB, operational risk, concentration-as-engine, the EWS engine with thresholds, the integrated stress chain, the regulatory return builder. None is in MAIIC's scope; the pieces the spec adopts from that suite are the ingestion, the shell, the audit workbooks, the macro feed and the scenario governance — not its prudential engines.

rep("| 6 | On `--verify`: runs the baselines of section 9 against the database and prints the table, PASS or FAIL per row, and exits non-zero on any FAIL | Yes |",

chain = '''
#### 6.10.1 The engine chain the bootstrap runs

The suite's bootstrap runs its engines in dependency order and treats the result as the proof of the installation. MAIIC's chain, in the order the modules depend on each other, with what each needs and how the bootstrap supplies it where a person would normally act:

| Order | Engine | Entry point | Needs | How the bootstrap meets it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Macro statistics | `macro:import-worldbank`; the WEO snapshot | Internet, or the committed snapshot | Snapshot under `docs/bootstrap/macro/` when the fetch fails (13.3) |
| 2 | Scenario set | the seeded first set of 15.8 | An approved set | Seeded as *proposed*; the bootstrap approves it under the automated label so the chain can run; it is not a MAIIC approval and the screen says so |
| 3 | Staging and SICR | `StagingClassifier` on each month's loan book | Governed thresholds; the loan book | Thresholds seeded; loan books built in step 5 |
| 4 | PD: transition matrices | `TransitionMatrixService`, cumulative | Twelve or more months of graded loan books | The 26 months from the landing zone |
| 5 | LGD | `CalculateLGDJob` and its chunks | Payments and collateral | Payments from the ledger; collateral from the register; runs synchronously |
| 6 | Forward-looking adjustment | the route in force (14.6) | An approved model, or an overlay | With no approvable model on a clean install the bootstrap runs the **manual overlay route at zero** and marks every post-FLI PD "no adjustment: bootstrap"; the regression route is used once a model has been approved by two people |
| 7 | ECL | `ifrs9:recalculate-ecl --pd=pd_post_fli`, the time-phased service | PD, LGD, EAD, stage, the EIR for discounting | Steps 3 to 6 and 9 |
| 8 | EIR: schedules | `eir:generate-schedules` | Terms, drawdowns, the take-on basis | Steps of 6.9; version 1 approved under the automated label |
| 9 | EIR: solve and revenue | `CalculateEirJob`, `eir:run-revenue {period}` | Approved schedules, fees, rates, the governed conventions | Step 8; fees from the charges table and the take-on workbook |
| 10 | GL reconciliation | `EirGlReconciliationService` | The trial balances | Landed in step 3 of the bootstrap |
| 11 | Stress testing | `StressTestingController` logic as a service | The ECL of step 7 | Run for the seeded scenario set |
| 12 | Reports and the audit workbooks | the 30 reports; `tools/compliance` | Everything above | Generated for the last period; the Baselines sheet reads the live figures |

Two orderings matter and are enforced: the ECL is discounted at the EIR, so step 9 runs before step 7 for each period (the chain runs 8 and 9 first, then 3 to 7, then 10 to 12); and the forward-looking adjustment runs once per scenario under the seeded weighting method of 15.5, so step 6 is a loop over the set of step 2.

Three engines are queued jobs today (LGD, EIR solve, revenue). Under `--run-engines` they run synchronously; on a server they still run through the queue, and the installation guide carries the worker command with a memory ceiling, because the suite found that a worker left on its default limit stops itself part-way through a full chain and later jobs wait in silence.

#### 6.10.2 Golden numbers

`--verify` checks the section 9 baselines and, once the engines have run, these figures. They are MAIIC's own, so a bootstrap on any server either reproduces them or fails:

| Golden number | Expected | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ECL at 31 December 2025, total and by stage | The audited impairment allowance in the 2025 financial statements | The AFS mapping workbook (`TB_AFS_MAP`), the impairment lines; the signed statements |
| ECL at 31 December 2024 | The audited 2024 allowance | The same workbook's December 2024 column |
| Contractual interest 2025, by loan GL | MWK 5,293,988,207.06 for January 2025 to July 2026 (section 9), split by month | The ledger |
| Interest income 2025 against the trial balance | The year-to-date tie, 83 of 83 account-months | Section 9 |
| Loan balances by GL at each year-end | The audited figures: 2024 and 2025 by GL | The AFS mapping workbook |
| The revenue shift 2024 and 2025 | Recorded on the first run that Dr Thom approves, then held as the number later builds must reproduce | The engine, once approved |

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-07 19:20:28 UTC)

Yes — and it is now in the spec (6.10.1 and 6.10.2, pushed as `9513587`). The command becomes `eir:bootstrap --fresh --with-client-inputs --build --run-engines --verify`, which is the suite's shape exactly.

## What `--run-engines` does

Runs the twelve engines in dependency order for every month from the first full month to the last in the pack, synchronously (queue driver set to `sync` for the run, so no worker is needed and nothing waits in silence). Where a person would normally act, the bootstrap supplies the precondition and labels it:

| Order | Engine | What the bootstrap has to supply |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Macro statistics | the committed snapshot when the World Bank fetch fails |
| 2 | Scenario set | the seeded first set, approved under the automated label (not a MAIIC approval, and the screen says so) |
| 3–5 | Staging/SICR, PD matrices, LGD | thresholds seeded; 26 months of loan books from the landing zone; payments from the ledger |
| 6 | Forward-looking | **the honest case**: on a clean install no regression model is approvable, so the chain runs the manual-overlay route at zero and marks every post-FLI PD "no adjustment: bootstrap"; the regression route takes over once two people have approved a model |
| 7 | ECL | discounted at the EIR, so 8–9 run first |
| 8–9 | EIR schedules, solve, revenue | version 1 schedules approved under the automated label |
| 10–12 | GL reconciliation, stress test, reports and audit workbooks | the landed trial balances; the seeded set; the Baselines sheet reads live figures |

Two orderings are enforced: EIR before ECL (the discount rate), and the FLI step loops over the scenarios under the "weight the ECL" method. The three queued jobs (LGD, EIR solve, revenue) run synchronously here and through the queue on a server — with the worker memory ceiling in the installation guide, because the suite found a default-limit worker stops itself part-way through a full chain.

## What `--verify` checks beyond the section 9 ties

MAIIC's own golden numbers: the **audited ECL allowance at 31 December 2025 and 2024** (from the AFS mapping workbook's impairment lines — the system's ECL must reproduce what Deloitte signed); the 2025 contractual interest by GL and month; the YTD interest-income tie; the audited loan balances by GL at each year-end; and, once Dr Thom approves the first run, **the 2024 and 2025 revenue shift** — written by that run and from then on failed by any build that changes it without a governed reason. That last row is how a golden number is born.

One caveat worth stating plainly: the ECL golden number is only as good as the staging and LGD inputs on the clean install matching what produced the audited figure; if the first bootstrap does not hit it, that is a finding to resolve, not a tolerance to widen.
