## CLAUDE  (2026-10-08 07:00:12 UTC)

The transmission mechanism — how a view of the economy becomes a change to each loan's PD — is, in MAIIC's system, a **multiplicative scalar derived from a regression on a loss proxy**. Here it is end to end, with what it implies and what the alternatives are.

## The chain, as the code runs it

**1. Economy → predicted loss proxy.** A regression fitted on history gives `proxy = intercept + slope × macro` (one macro variable as applied today; the full vector after the 14.5 repair). The proxy is a portfolio-level loss measure — an observed default rate or NPL ratio — not a loan's PD.

**2. Scenario → macro value per window.** For each forecast window *w* (0 = the base period, then 1, 2, … periods ahead) the macro value is the scenario-weighted figure: Σ value_s × probability_s across the scenario set (typed today; computed from the set under section 15).

**3. Predicted proxy → adjustment factor.** The factor is a *ratio to the base period*, not the predicted level:

`fli_adj(w) = predicted_proxy(w) / predicted_proxy(0) − 1`

So if the base-period model says 4.0 percent and the window-12 model says 4.6 percent, `fli_adj = +0.15`. Using a ratio rather than the level is what makes the factor transferable from a portfolio proxy to every loan: it says "losses in that environment are 15 percent above today's", whatever the loan's own starting PD.

**4. Factor → the loan, by stage.** Each loan takes one window:

- Stage 3: PD = 100 percent, no adjustment;
- Stage 1: the 12-month window;
- Stage 2: the window nearest its remaining life (lifetime PD);

and then **`pd_post_fli = pd_prefli × (1 + fli_adj)`**, floored at 0 and capped at 1.

**5. PD → ECL.** The ECL engine reads `pd_post_fli`; it may never write it back.

Every link is transparent, which is its virtue: a reviewer can follow one number from the GDP forecast to one loan's provision in five multiplications.

## What this mechanism implies

- **Proportional, the same for every loan.** A 15 percent uplift raises a 2 percent PD to 2.3 and a 40 percent PD to 46. Real credit risk is not proportional: a downturn moves weak borrowers far more than strong ones. The multiplier ignores that, which is why the cap at 100 percent is needed at all.
- **Linear in the macro variable.** A 10 percent fall in growth is assumed to move losses twice as much as a 5 percent fall. Loss rates in fact accelerate in downturns, which is one reason section 15 weights the ECL across scenarios rather than the macro path: the convexity is recovered at the scenario level even though the transmission inside each scenario is linear.
- **Lifetime via the nearest window.** A loan with 30 months left takes the window-30 factor if there is one, else the nearest. There is no term structure of PD inside the window — the same factor is applied to a flat PD, not to a marginal PD curve.
- **The proxy is the portfolio, not the segment.** One regression, one factor for every product group unless separate parameter sets are run per portfolio.

## The alternatives, and where they sit

| Method | Transmission | Where it is used |
|---|---|---|
| **Multiplicative scalar on a proxy ratio** (MAIIC today) | post = pre × (1 + adj) | MAIIC; FDH's "factor" kind, one of nine governed methods in the reference `AdjustmentMethods` (weighted statistic, annual difference or change, by-correlation variants, PD forecast, and three factor methods) |
| **Vasicek / Merton Z-shift** | Shift the latent systematic factor: PIT PD = Φ[(Φ⁻¹(TTC PD) − √ρ·Z) / √(1−ρ)], with Z from the macro regression; the shift is largest for mid-range PDs and naturally bounded at 0 and 1 | Banks with IRB-style models; the Basel single-factor framework |
| **Logit-linear PD model** | logit(PD) = α + β·macro; the move is in log-odds, so proportional in odds not in probability, bounded by construction | Common in regional banks; needs loan-level or grade-level default series |
| **Segment-specific scalars** | The same ratio method, one regression per portfolio or grade | Easy extension of MAIIC's method once section 14's proxy deriver gives segment proxies |

## What section 14 keeps and what it adds

The multiplicative scalar is kept, deliberately: it is what MAIIC's auditors have seen, it is explainable in one line, and with two years of core-banking history there is not the default-rate depth a Z-shift or a logit model would need to be more than a formula with invented inputs. What changes the *quality* of the transmission without changing its form is already in the spec: the guardrail (only a fit with the right sign, strength and significance may feed a factor; otherwise the PD holds), the full coefficient vector, lags and transforms, the proxy derived from MAIIC's own data, the factor computed once per scenario with the ECL weighted across them (which restores the convexity), the manual overlay with its own line, and lineage on every loan. The Z-shift or a logit model can be added later as a tenth governed method once the default history is long enough — the `fli_adjustment_route` setting is where that choice would live, and the reference engine already has the slot for it.

sec = '''### 14.7 How the adjustment reaches the PD: the transmission method

The route of 14.6 says where the adjustment comes from. The transmission method says how it moves a loan's PD once it exists. MAIIC has one method today, the multiplicative scalar; it is kept as the default, and the alternatives are built as governed choices with the data each one needs, so that the method can change when the history can support it without a change to the code.

**What the scalar does, and what it implies.** The adjustment is a ratio to the base period (predicted proxy in the window over predicted proxy today, less one), and the loan's PD is multiplied by one plus that ratio. It is proportional, the same for every loan whatever its starting PD, and linear in the macro variable. Real credit risk is neither: a downturn moves weak borrowers far more than strong ones, and loss rates accelerate as conditions worsen. The first effect is why the cap at 100 percent is needed at all; the second is recovered at the scenario level by weighting the ECL across scenarios (15.5) even though the transmission inside each scenario stays linear. With two years of core-banking history, the scalar is the honest choice: the richer methods below need a default-rate series the institution does not yet have.

**The governed setting**, `fli_transmission_method`, with the preconditions the guardrail checks before a method may run. A method whose preconditions are not met is declined with the reason and the PD holds, exactly as a failed fit is declined.

| Method | Transmission | Needs | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Multiplicative scalar on the proxy ratio** (seeded) | post-FLI PD = pre-FLI PD × (1 + adjustment); the adjustment is predicted proxy(window) / predicted proxy(base) − 1 | An approved fit, or an overlay | MAIIC's method; kept |
| Segment-specific scalar | The same, with one fit and one adjustment per portfolio or product group, from the segment proxies the deriver produces | A derivable proxy per segment (two or more periods each) | The natural next step; the deriver of 14.4 makes it possible |
| The nine reference methods | The suite's governed producers of a factor from a fit crossed with the scenario-weighted driver: the weighted statistic; the annual difference and the annual change in the driver; both scaled by the correlation; the absolute PD forecast from the equation; the forecast-over-base ratio (MAIIC's scalar is this one); and the two correlation-scaled difference and change variants | An approved fit with slope, intercept and correlation; the scenario-weighted driver | Ported as they are; selectable one at a time; each returns nothing rather than a fabricated figure when an input is undefined |
| Logit-linear PD model | logit(PD) = α + β × macro; the move is in log-odds, so proportional in the odds rather than the probability and bounded by construction | A grade-level or loan-level default series long enough to fit (the guardrail's minimum observations, at the grade level) | Available when the history allows; declined until then |
| Vasicek single-factor Z-shift | The through-the-cycle PD is moved through the latent systematic factor: PIT PD = Φ[(Φ⁻¹(TTC PD) − √ρ × Z) / √(1 − ρ)], with Z from the macro fit and ρ governed; the shift is largest for mid-range PDs and bounded by construction | A governed asset correlation ρ per portfolio and a Z series calibrated on a default-rate history | Available when the history allows; declined until then |

Whichever method is in force, three things do not change: Stage 3 is 100 percent; Stage 1 takes the 12-month window and Stage 2 the lifetime window; and the result is floored at 0 and capped at 100 percent. The method runs once per scenario under the weighting of 15.5, and the loan row records the method beside the route (14.8), so two loans adjusted under different methods in different periods can both be explained.

**Switching.** A change of method is a governed change with an effective date, under maker-checker, like every other setting. The first period run under a new method shows the ECL under both methods and the difference, which is itself a disclosure the auditors will want, as it is for the scenario weighting.

'''

## What 14.7 now says

**The transmission method is a governed choice** (`fli_transmission_method`), with the scalar kept as the seeded default and the honest reason why: with two years of core-banking history, the richer methods need a default-rate series MAIIC does not yet have. The alternatives are built, each behind its preconditions, declined with a reason until its data exists:

| Method | Needs |
|---|---|
| Multiplicative scalar on the proxy ratio (seeded) | an approved fit or an overlay |
| Segment-specific scalar | a derivable proxy per segment |
| The nine reference methods (weighted statistic, annual difference/change, correlation-scaled variants, absolute PD forecast, forecast-over-base ratio, the two FDH variants) | a fit with slope, intercept, correlation; the weighted driver |
| Logit-linear PD model | a grade-level default series long enough for the guardrail's minimum |
| Vasicek single-factor Z-shift | a governed asset correlation ρ (new setting, seeded 0.12) and a calibrated Z series |

Whatever the method: Stage 3 at 100%, Stage 1 the 12-month window, Stage 2 the lifetime window, floored and capped, run once per scenario, method recorded on the loan row.

**And your point — the system explains each method itself.** Every method has a **method card** on the FLI Adjustments screen and beside the setting in the Governance Centre, with five parts: what it does in plain sentences; the formula with its symbols named; what it implies (proportional or not, bounded or not, which loans it moves most); its **preconditions checked live against MAIIC's data** when the card opens, each met or not met with the deciding figure ("default-rate series: 24 months held, 36 needed"); and a **worked example on one real loan** showing pre-FLI PD, inputs, arithmetic and post-FLI PD under that method. A method with an unmet precondition cannot be selected, and the card says what has to be true first. The same cards appear in the help centre and the impairment audit workbook, so user, Board and auditor read the same words. The texts are seeded, versioned content, not strings in code.

Acceptance item 4 covers the cards; FL-3 grows to two days.
